hints: Notice the pair of products, an alcohol plus a carboxylate salt. This is the classic signature of alkaline hydrolysis of an ester.

Work backwards from the products. Methanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$, must come from a $\text{CH}_3\text{O}$ part, and ethanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^-$, must come from a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2$ part.
Now join those two fragments back together as $\text{acid part-O-alcohol part}$ to rebuild the original ester and match it to the list.
walkthrough:
**Spot the reaction type**

Great start, let's look at what is happening. An organic compound plus aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ giving an alcohol plus a sodium carboxylate is alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of an ester.

General rule:
$$\text{RCO}_2\text{R}' + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{RCO}_2\text{Na} + \text{R}'\text{OH}$$

**Split the products into two halves**

The alcohol tells us the alkyl group attached to oxygen. Here methanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$, means $\text{R}' = \text{CH}_3$.

The salt tells us the acid part. Here sodium ethanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$, means $\text{R} = \text{CH}_3$.

**Rebuild Y and check**

Put the acid part and alcohol part back together as an ester, $\text{RCO}_2\text{R}'$.

That gives:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{Na} + \text{CH}_3\text{OH}$$
This is methyl ethanoate, which matches the required products perfectly.

options.A: Correct. $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_3$ is methyl ethanoate. Alkaline hydrolysis splits it at the ester link to give $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ (methanol) and $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$ (sodium ethanoate), exactly as observed.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{HCO}_2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ is ethyl methanoate. Its hydrolysis would give ethanol, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, and sodium methanoate, $\text{HCO}_2\text{Na}$. Students who swap the acid and alcohol parts pick this.
options.C: Incorrect. $\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}_2\text{CHO}$ contains a carboxylic acid and an aldehyde, not an ester. With $\text{NaOH}$ the acid would be neutralised but you could not get methanol as a product.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ is a hydroxy carboxylic acid, not an ester. With $\text{NaOH}$ it would form a sodium salt plus water, not methanol plus sodium ethanoate.
